tool_args.old_string:
If hard pruning fails on SmolVLA because every token is indispensable, why does learned compression with cross-attention pooling succeed? The answer lies in the distinction between deletion and aggregation. Hard pruning applies a binary mask: selected tokens are kept verbatim, and the rest are discarded with their information permanently lost. Cross-attention pooling operates differently. A set of $M$ learned query vectors attends over all 128 source tokens through standard cross-attention, and each query computes a weighted sum across the full token set. Even when the output is compressed to $M = 32$ (a 75\% reduction in token count), every original token contributes to the compressed representation through its attention weight. No information is deleted; it is redistributed into fewer, higher-capacity vectors.

The experimental results confirm this mechanism and reveal an additional structure. Performance across four bottleneck widths ($M \in \{16, 32, 64, 96\}$) follows an inverted-U curve (Table~\ref{tab:smart_compress}). The peak occurs at $M \in \{32, 64\}$ (both 61.6\% SR), exceeding the uncompressed baseline by 16.8 percentage points. Reducing to $M = 16$ degrades to 55.8\%, and widening to $M = 96$ degrades further to 52.6\%. The inverted-U shape has a natural interpretation through the aggregation mechanism. At $M = 96$ (25\% compression), the bottleneck is too wide: the compressor can pass most token information through without learning selective aggregation, and the regularization benefit is minimal. At $M = 16$ (87.5\% compression), the bottleneck is too narrow: 16 queries cannot preserve sufficient spatial detail from 128 source tokens, and information loss begins to dominate despite the aggregation preserving all source contributions. The sweet spot at $M \in \{32, 64\}$ balances these two forces.

The inverted-U provides direct evidence that the performance improvement is driven by the compression bottleneck itself, not merely by the additional parameters. If the 22.2M parameters were the primary factor, performance would increase monotonically with $M$ (more queries = more capacity). Instead, $M = 96$ underperforms $M = 32$ despite having three times the query vectors, confirming that the bottleneck's regularization effect, forcing the compressor to select task-relevant features, is the dominant mechanism. We are training a passthrough control ($M = 128$, no compression) to further validate this interpretation; results pending.

This result carries a practical implication for VLA deployment. Architectures with aggressive spatial folding in their vision connectors are not inherently incompressible; they are incompressible under deletion-based methods. A learned compression module that aggregates rather than prunes can recover and even exceed baseline performance, offering a viable path to reduced inference cost without the cliff-edge failure that hard pruning induces.

If hard pruning fails on SmolVLA because every token is indispensable, why does learned compression with cross-attention pooling succeed? The answer lies in the distinction between deletion and re-encoding. Hard pruning applies a binary mask: selected tokens are kept verbatim, and the rest are discarded with their information permanently lost. Cross-attention pooling operates differently. A set of $M$ learned query vectors attends over all 128 source tokens through standard cross-attention, and each query computes a weighted sum across the full token set. Even when the output is compressed to $M = 32$ (a 75\% reduction in token count), every original token contributes to the output through its attention weight. No information is deleted; it is re-encoded into vectors that the downstream LLM can process more effectively.

The $M = 128$ passthrough control provides the critical test for identifying the source of the performance gain. At $M = 128$, the cross-attention module re-encodes all 128 source tokens into 128 query vectors with no token reduction. This configuration achieves 59.8\% SR (CI [55.4\%, 64.0\%]), statistically indistinguishable from $M = 32$ and $M = 64$ (both 61.6\%, CI [57.3\%, 65.8\%]). The gain over the uncompressed baseline (44.8\%) therefore originates from the cross-attention re-encoding itself, not from any compression bottleneck. The 22.2M-parameter cross-attention module transforms pixel-shuffle tokens into representations that the downstream LLM processes more effectively, regardless of whether the token count is reduced.

This result reframes the practical value of Smart Compress. Performance is approximately flat across $M \in \{32, 64, 128\}$ (59.8\%--61.6\%), with only $M = 16$ (55.8\%) showing a modest decline from information loss at extreme compression. $M = 96$ (52.6\%) is an outlier that likely reflects training dynamics rather than a systematic trend, given that both the narrower ($M = 64$) and wider ($M = 128$) configurations outperform it. Token reduction from 128 to 32 comes at no performance cost: compression is a deployment benefit (75\% KV-cache reduction, 6\% latency gain) layered on top of the re-encoding improvement, not a tradeoff against it.

This result carries a practical implication for VLA deployment. Architectures with aggressive spatial folding in their vision connectors are not inherently limited to their original performance; cross-attention re-encoding produces more effective token representations. When combined with compression ($M = 32$), this re-encoding delivers both a performance gain and a 75\% reduction in vision tokens, offering a viable path to improved accuracy and reduced inference cost without the cliff-edge failure that hard pruning induces.

Our findings carry a design-time message for VLA architects. The choice of vision connector determines not only the model's representational properties but also its amenability to inference-time optimization. Pixel-shuffle connectors offer aggressive spatial compression during training (1024 patches $\to$ 64 tokens per camera), reducing the LLM's input sequence length and training cost. This advantage comes at the cost of inference-time rigidity: once trained, the token count cannot be reduced further without retraining.

MLP projectors preserve per-token independence and allow post-hoc pruning with graceful degradation, but they produce longer token sequences (256 in OpenVLA) that increase training and inference cost. The tradeoff is between training efficiency (pixel-shuffle) and inference flexibility (MLP projector).

The attention entropy ratio provides a practical diagnostic for this tradeoff. Before deploying a VLA model, practitioners can compute the entropy ratio on a small calibration set (a single forward pass) to determine whether the model's vision tokens are amenable to post-hoc pruning. An entropy ratio close to 1.0 signals that the model relies uniformly on all tokens and that deletion-based compression will fail; in this case, learned aggregation (Smart Compress) is required. An entropy ratio substantially below 1.0 indicates that the model has developed selective attention and that token pruning can be applied with predictable, proportional degradation.

Even when the output is compressed to $M = 32$ (a 75\% reduction in token count), every original token contributes to the output through its attention weight. No information is deleted; it is re-encoded into vectors that the downstream LLM can process more effectively.

The $M = 128$ passthrough control provides the critical test for identifying the source of the performance gain. At $M = 128$, the cross-attention module re-encodes all 128 source tokens into 128 query vectors with no token reduction. This configuration achieves 59.8\% SR (CI [55.4\%, 64.0\%]), statistically indistinguishable from $M = 32$ and $M = 64$ (both 61.6\%, CI [57.3\%, 65.8\%]). The gain over the uncompressed baseline (44.8\%) therefore originates from the cross-attention re-encoding itself, not from any compression bottleneck. The 22.2M-parameter cross-attention module transforms pixel-shuffle tokens into representations that the downstream LLM processes more effectively, regardless of whether the token count is reduced.

This result reframes the practical value of Smart Compress. Performance is approximately flat across $M \in \{32, 64, 128\}$ (59.8\%--61.6\%), with only $M = 16$ (55.8\%) showing a modest decline from information loss at extreme compression. $M = 96$ (52.6\%) is an outlier that likely reflects training dynamics rather than a systematic trend, given that both the narrower ($M = 64$) and wider ($M = 128$) configurations outperform it. Token reduction from 128 to 32 comes at no performance cost: compression is a deployment benefit (75\% KV-cache reduction, 6\% latency gain) layered on top of the re-encoding improvement, not a tradeoff against it.

This result carries a practical implication for VLA deployment. Architectures with aggressive spatial folding in their vision connectors are not inherently limited to their original performance; cross-attention re-encoding produces more effective token representations. When combined with compression ($M = 32$), this re-encoding delivers both a performance gain and a 75\% reduction in vision tokens, offering a viable path to improved accuracy and reduced inference cost without the cliff-edge failure that hard pruning induces.
